newsitem.title: USA: Federal Reserve watching consumer prices as guide.
newsitem.headline: Federal Reserve watching consumer prices as guide.

text.p: The Federal Reserve, set on achieving long-term price stability, is close to adopting a monetary policy that would attempt to keep the government's measure of consumer price inflation within a specific target range, according to a Fed source.
The source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the policy, which relies on a measure of the Consumer Price Index, has been "informally adopted within the Fed."
Under the policy, the Fed considers a rate of inflation of between zero and 2 percent as measured by the core rate of the CPI to be non-inflationary.
The core rate of the CPI, which is prepared and released monthly by the Labour Department, excludes food and energy prices, which can cause wide fluctations in the index because of their volatility.
If such a policy were adopted, it would mark the first time that the Fed was using a specific measure as a guide in setting interest rates.

The Fed controls the discount rate, which is the rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks, and sets a target for the federal funds rate, which is the rate at which banks lend money to each other when they balance their accounts at the end of each business day.
Those rates in turn determine the rates at which banks and other institutions lend money to businesses and consumers.

The Fed's policy making arm, the Federal Open Market Committee is scheduled to meet Tuesday for its latest deliberations on interest rates, and speculation about what the panel might do has led to sporadic volatility in the stock and bond markets in recent weeks.
Many economists expect the Fed to raise the discount rate to 5.25 percent from 5.0 percent and to raise its target for the federal funds rate by a quarter point to 5.50 percent.
Eight of the 12 regional Fed district banks have asked the Fed to make such an increase in the federal funds rate as a means of warding off inflation.
The core rate of CPI rose 2.6 percent in the 12 months ended in August, a rate that would encourage the Fed to raise interest rates under the policy described by the Fed source.

When the Fed last moved on interest rates -- it cut the federal funds and discount rates by a quarter point on Jan. 31 -- it did so without dissent and with six Fed banks requesting a cut in the largely symbolic discount rate.
One reason for targeting CPI is the loss of usefulness of policy references such as the monetary aggregates.
Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan, a voting member of the FOMC, commented on the notion of a numerical target as a guideline for monetary policy as early as 1992.
The Fed's current view on targeting core CPI is in line with a CPI range first spelled out by New York Fed President William McDonough in a March 21 speech.

McDonough defined U.S. price stability as being in a range between 0.5 percent and 2.0 percent on CPI to allow for the upward bias believed to exist in the imperfect -- but most publicised -- measure of U.S. inflation.
According to another source, New York Fed Director of Research Frederic Mishkin and Head of the Markets Group Peter Fisher contributed to formulating that range.
The notion has since received the support of long-time FOMC members such as San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry.
A New York Fed spokesman said the bank had no comment on the notion of a numerical target for monetary policy or the impact of McDonough's views within the Fed.

The Fed is considering targeting core CPI regardless of the fate of legislation sponsored by Sen. Connie Mack, R-Fla., that would establish price stability as the Fed's main goal and require the central bank to use a numerical target toward that goal.
The Fed's existing dual mandate is to seek both full employment and price stability.

The FOMC discussed Mack's bill at its Sept. 26, 1995, meeting, noting members' "initial reaction was favourable in regard to the overall thrust of the bill...(that) would restructure the monetary policy requirements to permit the Congress to carry out its oversight responsibilities more effectively."
The CPI is a key issue on more than one account.
A low CPI would not only help drive U.S. long-term market rates lower along with declining inflation expectations, it would also reduce government spending on a number of inflation-indexed outlays.
